phase: 1 — lazy min-heap top-K (replaces the O(C·log C) full sort)

hardware.note: mobile CPU, thermal-throttled, single-thread; absolute numbers understate a server; measured under reduced container load

method: end-to-end query latency for ORDER BY embedding <-> q LIMIT 10, best-of-5 runs × 2 passes (min mean), 200 queries seed 7; baseline = theo-db:m35 (full sort), optimized = theo-db:m36 (lazy heap); IDENTICAL data/index/probes on both
recall: IDENTICAL by construction — the heap emits the same (dist,tid) ascending order as the old sort (byte-identical top-K); proven by 61 coexistence tests returning the same kNN ids (test_index_am/test_hnsw_structured/test_reloption/test_ann_index/test_sbq_index)
measurement_first_finding: the M36 profiler (THEODB_SCAN_PROFILE) falsified the original 'quantize the distance' premise: distance is ~15% of scan cost; the bottlenecks are reads (~44-51%) and sort (~35-41%). Phase 1 attacks sort.

profiler_sort_phase.reduction: ~10-13× on the sort/heapify phase (O(C·log C) full sort → O(C) heapify; per-pop O(log C)×k moved to amgettuple, bounded by the executor LIMIT)

verdict.end_to_end_speedup: 1.38–2.07× (grows with candidate count / probes), recall identical
verdict.closes_scann_gap: partially — this attacks the ~35-41% sort phase. The remaining ~44-51% reads phase is M36 Phase 2 (smaller quantized codes to cut I/O + f32 rerank). The full ScaNN gap (~25×, M33) also needs harder candidate pruning. HONEST: this is a real ~1.4-2.1× scan speedup at preserved recall, NOT '25× from the sort alone'.

reproduction: PGPORT=<port> python3 benchmarks/run_m36_scan.py --n 200000 --probes 50 --k 10 --runs 5 --label <sort|heap>  (baseline on theo-db:m35, optimized on theo-db:m36)
